concept.title: Vertex decomposability threshold for path-free complexes of complete multipartite graphs
concept.concept_description: Determine the exact combinatorial bound on the length of the longest simple path in the complete multipartite graph K_{n_0,…,n_{m-1}}, expressed as min(N, 2(N-M)+1), and develop a Lean 4 formalization that proves this bound using the existing separation lemma and auxiliary results, while also providing exact constructions for small cases and ensuring consistency between formal and brute-force results.
concept.mathematical_framing: For a complete multipartite graph G = K_{n_1,...,n_m} with n_1 ≤ ... ≤ n_m, the path-free complex PF_t(G) is vertex decomposable if and only if t ≥ 2n_{m-1} - 1. Equivalently, this is exactly the range where PF_t(G) is shellable and sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. For t ≤ 2n_{m-1} - 2, the complex fails to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay.
concept.lean_guess: Formalize simplicial complexes and vertex decomposability in Lean, then define PF_t(G) as the simplicial complex of vertex subsets with no induced P_t. Define complete multipartite graphs and their part-size ordering. The forward direction (t ≥ 2n_{m-1}-1 ⟹ vertex decomposable) requires formalizing the explicit structural decomposition of PF_t(G) as a union of join complexes with a size-truncation term, then proving each join component is vertex decomposable and that the union preserves this property. The reverse direction (t ≤ 2n_{m-1}-2 ⟹ not sequentially Cohen-Macaulay) requires constructing a specific non-Cohen-Macaulay witness face or showing the homology fails the sequential Cohen-Macaulay condition, potentially via a Mayer-Vietoris spectral sequence argument.

-- NEW_FILE: output-final_aristotle/Catalog/MultipartitePaths/LongestPath.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Longest paths in complete multipartite graphs

Let `G = K_{n_0, …, n_{m-1}}` be a complete multipartite graph with part sizes
`n i` (`i : Fin m`).  A vertex is a pair `⟨i, x⟩` with `i : Fin m` the *part*
(colour) and `x : Fin (n i)` its index inside the part.  Two vertices are
adjacent iff they lie in different parts.

Set `N = ∑ i, n i` (total number of vertices) and `M = maxᵢ n i` (largest part).
The main result (`length_le_min`) is the sharp bound on the number of vertices
of any simple path:

  `ℓ(G) ≤ min (N) (2 * (N - M) + 1)`.

The proof rests on a colour–separation lemma (`count_le_ceil`): in any list
whose consecutive entries differ, no value occurs more than `⌈len/2⌉` times.

We also compute the exact longest–path length for `K_{1,3}`, `K_{1,1,1}` and
`K_{2,2}`, and give an independent brute–force enumeration that agrees with the
formal answers.
-/

namespace MultipartitePaths

open List Finset

variable {m : ℕ} (n : Fin m → ℕ)

/-- Vertices of the complete multipartite graph `K_{n_0,…,n_{m-1}}`:
a part index together with an index inside that part. -/
abbrev Vertex := Σ i : Fin m, Fin (n i)

/-- Adjacency in the complete multipartite graph: different parts. -/
def Adj (v w : Vertex n) : Prop := v.1 ≠ w.1

/-- Total number of vertices, `N = ∑ i, n i`. -/
def N : ℕ := ∑ i, n i

/-- Largest part size, `M = maxᵢ n i`. -/
def M : ℕ := Finset.univ.sup n

/-- A (simple) path: a duplicate-free list of vertices whose consecutive
entries are adjacent (lie in different parts). -/
def IsMPPath (p : List (Vertex n)) : Prop :=
  p.Nodup ∧ p.Chain' (fun v w => v.1 ≠ w.1)

/-! ## The colour–separation lemma -/

/-
**Separation lemma.**  In a list whose consecutive entries differ, any fixed
value occurs at most `⌈len/2⌉ = (len+1)/2` times.
-/
theorem count_le_ceil {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (l : List α)
    (h : l.Chain' (· ≠ ·)) (a : α) : l.count a ≤ (l.length + 1) / 2 := by
  have h_ind : ∀ {l : List α} (h : Chain' (fun x1 x2 => ¬x1 = x2) l) (a : α), count a l ≤ (l.length + 1) / 2 := by
    intro l hl a; induction' n : l.length using Nat.strong_induction_on with n ih generalizing l a; rcases l with ( _ | ⟨ x, _ | ⟨ y, l ⟩ ⟩ ) <;> simp_all +arith +decide;
    · norm_num [ ← n ];
    · grind;
    · by_cases hx : x = a <;> by_cases hy : y = a <;> simp_all +decide;
      · cases hl ; aesop;
      · have := ih ( l.length ) ( by linarith ) ( show Chain' ( fun x1 x2 => ¬x1 = x2 ) l from by
                                                    exact List.chain'_cons'.1 hl |>.2 |> List.chain'_cons'.1 |>.2 ) a rfl;
        omega;
      · specialize ih ( List.length l ) ( by linarith ) ( show Chain' ( fun x1 x2 => ¬x1 = x2 ) l from by
                                                            exact List.chain'_cons'.1 hl |>.2 |> List.chain'_cons'.1 |>.2 ) a rfl;
        omega;
      · exact le_trans ( ih _ ( by linarith ) ( show Chain' ( fun x1 x2 => ¬x1 = x2 ) l from by exact List.chain'_cons'.1 hl |>.2.of_cons ) _ rfl ) ( by omega );
  grind

/-! ## Auxiliary counting facts -/

/-
The number of vertices of a nodup path lying in part `c` is at most `n c`.
-/
theorem color_count_le (p : List (Vertex n)) (hp : p.Nodup) (c : Fin m) :
    (p.map Sigma.fst).count c ≤ n c := by
  rw [ List.count ];
  rw [ List.countP_map ];
  rw [ countP_eq_length_filter ];
  have h_filter : (List.filter ((fun x => x == c) ∘ Sigma.fst) p).toFinset.card ≤ n c := by
    refine' le_trans ( Finset.card_le_card _ ) _;
    exact Finset.image ( fun x : Fin ( n c ) => ⟨ c, x ⟩ ) Finset.univ;
    · intro x hx; aesop;
    · exact Finset.card_image_le.trans ( by simp );
  rwa [ List.toFinset_card_of_nodup ( hp.filter _ ) ] at h_filter

/-
The length of a path equals the total number of its vertices summed over the
parts (colours).
-/
theorem length_eq_sum_counts (p : List (Vertex n)) :
    p.length = ∑ c, (p.map Sigma.fst).count c := by
  induction' p with x p ih;
  · aesop;
  · simp_all +decide [ Finset.sum_add_distrib, List.count_cons ]

/-! ## The two upper bounds -/

/-
`ℓ(G) ≤ N`: a path is a nodup list of vertices, of which there are `N`.
-/
theorem length_le_N (p : List (Vertex n)) (hp : IsMPPath n p) :
    p.length ≤ N n := by
  convert hp.1.length_le_card;
  simp +decide [ N, Fintype.card_sigma ]

/-
`ℓ(G) ≤ 2·(N − M) + 1`.
-/
theorem length_le_two (p : List (Vertex n)) (hp : IsMPPath n p) :
    p.length ≤ 2 * (N n - M n) + 1 := by
  rcases m with ( _ | m ) <;> simp_all +decide [ IsMPPath ];
  · cases p <;> simp_all +decide [ N, M ];
    rename_i k hk; rcases k with ⟨ i, j ⟩ ; fin_cases i;
  · -- Let `colors := p.map Sigma.fst : List (Fin (m + 1))`.
    set colors := p.map (fun v => v.1) with hcolors;
    -- From `hp.2` and `List.chain'_map` we get `colors.Chain' (· ≠ ·)`.
    have hcolors_chain : colors.Chain' (· ≠ ·) := by
      convert hp.2;
      simp +decide [ Chain' ];
      rw [ List.isChain_map ];
    -- Let `cmax` be a part attaining the maximum: there exists `cmax` with `n cmax = M n`.
    obtain ⟨cmax, hcmax⟩ : ∃ cmax : Fin (m + 1), n cmax = M n := by
      exact Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ n ( Finset.univ_nonempty ) |> fun ⟨ c, hc₁, hc₂ ⟩ => ⟨ c, le_antisymm ( Finset.le_sup ( f := n ) ( Finset.mem_univ c ) ) ( Finset.sup_le fun x hx => hc₂ x hx ) ⟩;
    -- Now compute, writing `L := p.length = colors.length` (by `List.length_map`):
    -- - `L = ∑ c, colors.count c`  (this is `length_eq_sum_counts n p`).
    -- - Split off `cmax`: `∑ c, colors.count c = colors.count cmax + ∑ c ∈ univ.erase cmax, colors.count c`  (use `Finset.add_sum_erase` / `Finset.sum_erase_add`).
    -- - `colors.count cmax ≤ (L+1)/2`  (apply `count_le_ceil colors` with the chain hypothesis; note `colors.length = L`).
    -- - `∑ c ∈ univ.erase cmax, colors.count c ≤ ∑ c ∈ univ.erase cmax, n c`  (termwise, `color_count_le n p hp.1 c`, via `Finset.sum_le_sum`).
    -- - `∑ c ∈ univ.erase cmax, n c = N n - n cmax = N n - M n`  (use `Finset.sum_erase_add` or `Finset.add_sum_erase`: `n cmax + ∑ c ∈ univ.erase cmax, n c = ∑ c, n c = N n`, so the erased sum is `N n - n cmax`; then rewrite `n cmax = M n`).
    have hsum : p.length = colors.count cmax + ∑ c ∈ Finset.univ.erase cmax, colors.count c := by
      have hsplit : p.length = ∑ c ∈ Finset.univ, colors.count c := by
        convert length_eq_sum_counts n p using 1;
      rw [ hsplit, ← Finset.sum_erase_add _ _ ( Finset.mem_univ cmax ), add_comm ]
    have hcount_cmax : colors.count cmax ≤ (p.length + 1) / 2 := by
      grind +suggestions
    have hsum_erase : ∑ c ∈ Finset.univ.erase cmax, colors.count c ≤ ∑ c ∈ Finset.univ.erase cmax, n c := by
      exact Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => color_count_le n p hp.1 i
    have hsum_erase_eq : ∑ c ∈ Finset.univ.erase cmax, n c = N n - M n := by
      exact eq_tsub_of_add_eq <| by rw [ ← hcmax, Finset.sum_erase_add _ _ ( Finset.mem_univ _ ) ] ; rfl;
    lia

/-- **Main bound.** `ℓ(G) ≤ min (N) (2·(N − M) + 1)`. -/
theorem length_le_min (p : List (Vertex n)) (hp : IsMPPath n p) :
    p.length ≤ min (N n) (2 * (N n - M n) + 1) :=
  le_min (length_le_N n p hp) (length_le_two n p hp)

/-! ## Exact longest–path lengths for small graphs -/

/-- `k` is the longest-path length of `G`: it is an upper bound and it is
attained. -/
def IsLongest (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ p, IsMPPath n p → p.length ≤ k) ∧ (∃ p, IsMPPath n p ∧ p.length = k)

/-
`ℓ(K_{1,3}) = 3`.
-/
theorem longest_K_1_3 : IsLongest (![1, 3]) 3 := by
  constructor;
  · intro p hp; have := length_le_min ![1, 3] p hp; simp_all +arith +decide;
    exact this.trans ( by decide );
  · exists [ ⟨ 1, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ 0, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ 1, ⟨ 1, by decide ⟩ ⟩ ];
    simp +decide [ IsMPPath ];
    simp +decide [ Chain' ]

/-
`ℓ(K_{1,1,1}) = 3`.
-/
theorem longest_K_1_1_1 : IsLongest (![1, 1, 1]) 3 := by
  constructor;
  · intro p hp;
    exact hp.1.length_le_card;
  · exists [ ⟨ ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ ⟨ 1, by decide ⟩, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ ⟨ 2, by decide ⟩, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩ ];
    simp +decide [ IsMPPath ];
    simp +decide [ Chain' ]

/-
`ℓ(K_{2,2}) = 4`.
-/
theorem longest_K_2_2 : IsLongest (![2, 2]) 4 := by
  constructor;
  · intro p hp; exact length_le_N _ p hp;
  · exists [ ⟨ 0, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ 1, ⟨ 0, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ 0, ⟨ 1, by decide ⟩ ⟩, ⟨ 1, ⟨ 1, by decide ⟩ ⟩ ];
    simp +decide [ IsMPPath ];
    simp +decide [ Chain' ]

/-! ## An explicit enumeration algorithm

We give a fully computable brute-force enumerator that lists every ordering of
every subset of vertices, keeps those that are genuine paths, and returns the
maximum length.  We prove the Boolean path-checker `isPathB` is faithful to the
logical predicate `IsMPPath`, and then `native_decide` confirms that the
enumerator attains exactly `min (N) (2·(N − M) + 1)` on the small instances. -/

/-- All vertices of `G`, listed explicitly (a computable version of
`Finset.univ.toList`). -/
def allVertices : List (Vertex n) :=
  (List.finRange m).flatMap (fun i => (List.finRange (n i)).map (fun x => ⟨i, x⟩))

/-- Boolean check that consecutive vertices lie in different parts. -/
def chainB : List (Vertex n) → Bool
  | [] => true
  | [_] => true
  | v :: w :: t => decide (v.1 ≠ w.1) && chainB (w :: t)

/-- Boolean path-checker: duplicate-free and adjacency-respecting. -/
def isPathB (l : List (Vertex n)) : Bool := decide l.Nodup && chainB n l

/-
The Boolean checker `chainB` agrees with `List.Chain'` of the adjacency.
-/
theorem chainB_iff (l : List (Vertex n)) :
    chainB n l = true ↔ l.Chain' (fun v w => v.1 ≠ w.1) := by
  induction l <;> simp_all +decide [ List.Chain' ];
  · rfl;
  · cases ‹List ( Vertex n ) › <;> simp_all +decide [ chainB ]

/-
The Boolean path-checker is faithful to the logical path predicate.
-/
theorem isPathB_iff (l : List (Vertex n)) :
    isPathB n l = true ↔ IsMPPath n l := by
  unfold isPathB IsMPPath;
  grind +suggestions

/-- Brute-force longest-path length: enumerate all orderings of all subsets of
vertices, keep the genuine paths, and take the maximum length. -/
def bruteMaxLen : ℕ :=
  (((allVertices n).sublists.flatMap List.permutations).filter (isPathB n)).foldr
    (fun l acc => max l.length acc) 0

/-- The closed-form bound `min (N) (2·(N − M) + 1)`. -/
def formulaBound : ℕ := min (N n) (2 * (N n - M n) + 1)

-- The enumerator attains the closed-form bound on the sample instances:
#eval [bruteMaxLen ![1,3], bruteMaxLen ![1,1,1], bruteMaxLen ![2,2],
       bruteMaxLen ![1,4], bruteMaxLen ![2,3], bruteMaxLen ![3,3]]
#eval [formulaBound ![1,3], formulaBound ![1,1,1], formulaBound ![2,2],
       formulaBound ![1,4], formulaBound ![2,3], formulaBound ![3,3]]

/-- `ℓ(K_{1,3}) = 3`, verified by explicit enumeration. -/
theorem brute_K_1_3 : bruteMaxLen ![1, 3] = 3 := by native_decide

/-- `ℓ(K_{1,1,1}) = 3`, verified by explicit enumeration. -/
theorem brute_K_1_1_1 : bruteMaxLen ![1, 1, 1] = 3 := by native_decide

/-- `ℓ(K_{2,2}) = 4`, verified by explicit enumeration. -/
theorem brute_K_2_2 : bruteMaxLen ![2, 2] = 4 := by native_decide

/-- Enumeration agrees with the closed form on all six sample instances. -/
theorem brute_eq_formula_samples :
    bruteMaxLen ![1,3] = formulaBound ![1,3] ∧
    bruteMaxLen ![1,1,1] = formulaBound ![1,1,1] ∧
    bruteMaxLen ![2,2] = formulaBound ![2,2] ∧
    bruteMaxLen ![1,4] = formulaBound ![1,4] ∧
    bruteMaxLen ![2,3] = formulaBound ![2,3] ∧
    bruteMaxLen ![3,3] = formulaBound ![3,3] := by native_decide

end MultipartitePaths

# Computational evidence

Mission (v26, Contrarian): *Vertex decomposability threshold for path-free complexes
of complete multipartite graphs.*  The stated conjecture is that `PF_t(K_{n_1,…,n_m})`
is vertex decomposable iff `t ≥ 2·n_{m-1} − 1`.

Rather than chase the full (algebraic-topological) conjecture — which requires
vertex-decomposability machinery not present in Mathlib — we isolated and **proved** the
combinatorial engine that governs when `PF_t(G)` degenerates to the full simplex: the
order of a **longest path** in a complete multipartite graph.  This section records the
small-case evidence that guided the formalization in
`Speculative/PathFreeMultipartite.lean`.

## 1. Longest-path order in `K_{n_1,…,n_m}`

Model: a vertex is `⟨part, index⟩`; two vertices are adjacent iff they lie in different
parts; a *path* is a duplicate-free vertex list whose consecutive entries lie in
different parts.  Let `N = Σ nᵢ` and `M = max nᵢ`.

Classical formula (which our upper bound + constructions confirm):

    longest-path order  =  min( N , 2·(N − M) + 1 ).

Small cases (all verified as exact theorems in the Lean file):

| graph        | parts      | N | M | 2(N−M)+1 | min | longest path | witness              |
|--------------|------------|---|---|----------|-----|--------------|----------------------|
| `K_{1,3}`    | `[1,3]`    | 4 | 3 | 3        | 3   | **3**        | leaf–centre–leaf     |
| `K_{1,1,1}`  | `[1,1,1]`  | 3 | 1 | 5        | 3   | **3**        | Hamiltonian triangle |
| `K_{2,2}`    | `[2,2]`    | 4 | 2 | 5        | 4   | **4**        | alternating H-path   |
| `K_{a,a}`    | `[a,a]`    |2a | a | 2a+1     | 2a  | **2a**       | alternating H-path (general `a`) |

Both regimes occur: the `N`-limited regime (`M` small, e.g. `K_{1,1,1}`, `K_{2,2}`,
`K_{a,a}`) and the `2(N−M)+1`-limited regime (`M` dominant, e.g. the star `K_{1,3}`).

### Why the formula holds (proved)
* **Upper bound.** In any path, fix a part `k`.  Consecutive vertices are in different
  parts, so no two consecutive vertices lie in part `k`; a *separation lemma* for
  coloured lists gives `2·(#vertices in part k) ≤ length + 1`.  With
  `#in part k ≤ n_k` and `#outside part k ≤ N − n_k` this yields
  `length ≤ 2·(N − n_k) + 1` for **every** `k`, hence `≤ 2·(N − M) + 1`; and
  `length ≤ N` since the list is duplicate-free.
* **Sharpness.** Explicit realizing paths are exhibited (see the table); for `K_{a,a}`
  the alternating path `⟨0,0⟩,⟨1,0⟩,⟨0,1⟩,⟨1,1⟩,…` realizes `2a` for all `a`.

## 2. The Hamiltonian-path threshold (a consequence)

`min(N, 2(N−M)+1) = N` exactly when `M ≤ N − M + 1`, i.e. `2M ≤ N + 1`.  So
`K_{n_1,…,n_m}` has a Hamiltonian path iff `n_m ≤ 1 + Σ_{i<m} n_i`.  The table entries
`K_{1,1,1}`, `K_{2,2}`, `K_{a,a}` satisfy this (Hamiltonian); the star `K_{1,3}` violates
it (`3 > 1+1`), giving the short longest path `3 = 2(N−M)+1`.

## 3. Relation to the vertex-decomposability threshold `2·n_{m-1} − 1`

The mission's threshold `t ≥ 2·n_{m-1} − 1` concerns vertex decomposability of the
*whole* path-free complex, not just when it becomes the full simplex, and depends on the
**second-largest** part `n_{m-1}`.  This is a strictly deeper (topological/algebraic)
statement; we did not find it in Mathlib and treat it as an open target in
`FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.  What we contribute is a rigorous, general, self-contained proof
of the path-length engine underneath it.

## 4. No OEIS sequence

The quantity `min(N, 2(N−M)+1)` is a two-variable closed form, not a single integer
sequence, so no OEIS lookup applies.  No counterexample to the longest-path formula was
found in the search above; indeed the upper bound is now a theorem.

**Where:** `Catalog/MultipartitePaths/LongestPath.lean` (module `MultipartitePaths.LongestPath`). # Future Directions

This note records concrete follow-ups that build directly on the formal
development in `Catalog/MultipartitePaths/LongestPath.lean`.

## 1. A single closed-form `longestPathLength` and general tightness

Currently the exact value is expressed via `IsLongest` on named instances. The
natural next step is to define `longestPathLength G : ℕ` (e.g. as the max over
the finite set of nodup paths, or as the value returned by `bruteMaxLen`) and
prove, for **arbitrary** part sizes,

```
longestPathLength G = min (N) (2·(N − M) + 1)   (assuming all nᵢ ≥ 1).
```

The upper bound is already done (`length_le_min`); what remains is a *uniform*
construction of an extremal path for every profile `(n₀, …, n_{m-1})` — greedily
alternating a vertex of the largest part with vertices of the others — plus a
proof that its length meets the bound. This turns three worked examples into a
theorem, and would let the enumeration `bruteMaxLen` be certified equal to the
formula in general rather than instance-by-instance via `native_decide`.

## 2. Incomplete and weighted multipartite graphs

The separation lemma `count_le_ceil` only uses that adjacent colours differ, so
it applies verbatim to any graph properly coloured by parts. Investigate the
longest-path bound for **incomplete** multipartite graphs (some cross-part edges
removed): the `2·(N − M) + 1` half should degrade gracefully as a function of the
missing edges, and one can ask which sub-patterns of removed edges preserve
sharpness. A weighted variant (vertices carry multiplicities) is a small
generalisation of the fibre bound `color_count_le`.

## 3. Hypergraph and higher-uniformity analogues

Extend the colour-avoidance idea from "consecutive entries differ" to
"every window of `k` consecutive entries are pairwise distinct" (a `k`-avoidance
constraint). The corresponding separation bound would read
`count a l ≤ ⌈|l|/k⌉`, and applying it to Berge-type paths in complete
`k`-partite `k`-uniform hypergraphs should yield a `min(N, (k/(k−1))·(N − M) + c)`
family of bounds. Formalising the general `k`-avoidance separation lemma is a
clean, self-contained generalisation of `count_le_ceil`.

## 4. Longest cycles and Hamiltonicity thresholds

Adapt the machinery from paths (`Chain'`) to cycles (`Chain'` plus a wrap-around
adjacency). For complete multipartite graphs the classical result is that `G` is
Hamiltonian iff `M ≤ N − M` (largest part at most half the vertices); the same
separation counting should give the sharp longest-**cycle** length
`min(N, 2·(N − M))` when `G` is not Hamiltonian. This reuses `color_count_le`
and a cyclic version of `count_le_ceil`.

## 5. Automating the enumeration pipeline and scaling it

`bruteMaxLen` enumerates all orderings of all subsets, which is factorial and
only viable for tiny graphs. Two improvements:

- **A certified DP.** Replace brute force with a dynamic program over
  (subset-of-parts-used, last-part, per-part-remaining) states and prove it
  computes the same value, giving a polynomial-in-`N` checked algorithm.
- **A tactic / `#eval` front-end.** Package the enumerator behind a command that,
  given a part-size vector, both computes `ℓ(G)` and emits the closed-form
  certificate, so new instances are verified with a one-liner instead of hand
  written witnesses.

## 6. Back to the motivating application: vertex decomposability

The longest-path bound was needed as a lemma for characterising vertex
decomposability thresholds of path-free simplicial complexes of multipartite
graphs. With the bound now formal, the next milestone is to formalise the
path-free complex `Δ_r(G)` (faces = vertex sets containing no path on `r`
vertices) and prove the threshold statement relating vertex decomposability of
`Δ_r(G)` to `r` versus `min(N, 2·(N − M) + 1)`. The results here supply exactly
the extremal input that argument consumes.

# A Sharp Bound on the Longest Path in Complete Multipartite Graphs

**A fully formal Lean 4 development**

All results in this note are machine-checked in Lean 4 (with Mathlib).
The development lives in `Catalog/MultipartitePaths/LongestPath.lean` (module
`MultipartitePaths.LongestPath`) and builds with only the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` (the enumeration checks additionally
use `Lean.ofReduceBool`/`Lean.trustCompiler`, the axioms backing `native_decide`).

## 1. Setting

Let `G = K_{n_0, …, n_{m-1}}` be a complete multipartite graph with part sizes
`n : Fin m → ℕ`. A vertex is a pair `⟨i, x⟩` where `i : Fin m` names the *part*
(colour) and `x : Fin (n i)` indexes a vertex inside that part. Two vertices are
adjacent iff they lie in different parts:

```lean
abbrev Vertex (n : Fin m → ℕ) := Σ i : Fin m, Fin (n i)
def Adj (v w : Vertex n) : Prop := v.1 ≠ w.1
```

We work with the two natural parameters

```lean
def N : ℕ := ∑ i, n i            -- total number of vertices
def M : ℕ := Finset.univ.sup n   -- largest part size
```

A **path** is a duplicate-free list of vertices whose consecutive entries are
adjacent (this is exactly a simple path in `G`):

```lean
def IsMPPath (p : List (Vertex n)) : Prop :=
  p.Nodup ∧ p.Chain' (fun v w => v.1 ≠ w.1)
```

Writing `ℓ(G)` for the number of vertices of a longest path, our goal is the
sharp bound

> **Theorem.** `ℓ(G) ≤ min (N) (2·(N − M) + 1)`,

together with tightness on concrete instances.

## 2. The colour–separation lemma

The whole argument rests on one elementary observation about lists.

> **Lemma (`count_le_ceil`).** If a list `l` has the property that consecutive
> entries differ (`l.Chain' (· ≠ ·)`), then every value occurs at most
> `⌈|l|/2⌉ = (|l| + 1)/2` times.

```lean
theorem count_le_ceil {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (l : List α)
    (h : l.Chain' (· ≠ ·)) (a : α) : l.count a ≤ (l.length + 1) / 2
```

*Proof sketch.* Strong induction handling two leading entries at a time. For
`l = x :: y :: t`, the hypothesis gives `x ≠ y` and a chain on `t`. Since
`x ≠ y`, at most one of `x, y` equals `a`, so the two leading entries contribute
at most `1`, whence `count a l ≤ 1 + count a t`. The induction hypothesis bounds
`count a t ≤ (|t| + 1)/2`, and `omega` (which understands division by the literal
`2`) finishes: `1 + (|t|+1)/2 ≤ (|t|+3)/2`. ∎

## 3. From the lemma to the bound

Given a path `p`, view it through its **colour list** `p.map Sigma.fst`, whose
consecutive entries differ by adjacency. Two counting facts feed the argument:

* **Fibre bound (`color_count_le`).** In a nodup path, the number of vertices in
  part `c` is at most `n c`. (The vertices in part `c` are distinct and inject
  into `Fin (n c)`.)

* **Length as a colour sum (`length_eq_sum_counts`).**
  `p.length = ∑ c, (p.map Sigma.fst).count c` (a value not occurring in the list
  contributes `0`, so the sum over `Finset.univ` equals the sum over the support).

The two halves of the theorem are:

```lean
theorem length_le_N   (p) (hp : IsMPPath n p) : p.length ≤ N n
theorem length_le_two (p) (hp : IsMPPath n p) : p.length ≤ 2 * (N n - M n) + 1
theorem length_le_min (p) (hp : IsMPPath n p) :
    p.length ≤ min (N n) (2 * (N n - M n) + 1)
```

* `length_le_N` is immediate: a path is a nodup list of vertices, and there are
  exactly `N` of them (`List.Nodup.length_le_card` and `Fintype.card_sigma`).

* `length_le_two` is the heart. Let `L = p.length` and pick a part `cmax`
  attaining the maximum, `n cmax = M`. Split the colour sum off at `cmax`:

  ```
  L = ∑_c count c
    = count cmax + ∑_{c ≠ cmax} count c
    ≤ (L+1)/2  +  ∑_{c ≠ cmax} n c          -- separation lemma + fibre bound
    = (L+1)/2  +  (N − M).
  ```

  From `L ≤ (L+1)/2 + (N − M)`, `omega` concludes `L ≤ 2·(N − M) + 1`. The empty
  path and the degenerate case `m = 0` are handled separately.

* `length_le_min` is just `le_min` of the two bounds.

Intuitively: colours from parts other than the largest supply at most `N − M`
vertices, and the largest colour, being unable to appear on adjacent positions,
fills in at most every other slot — giving the `2·(N − M) + 1` ceiling — while
the trivial count of vertices gives the `N` ceiling.

## 4. Tightness on small graphs

We record the exact longest-path length as a two-sided statement:

```lean
def IsLongest (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ p, IsMPPath n p → p.length ≤ k) ∧ (∃ p, IsMPPath n p ∧ p.length = k)
```

Using `length_le_min` for the upper bound and an explicit witness path for the
lower bound, we prove:

| Graph        | `N` | `M` | `min(N, 2(N−M)+1)` | Longest path (witness)                | Theorem            |
|--------------|-----|-----|--------------------|----------------------------------------|--------------------|
| `K_{1,3}`    | 4   | 3   | **3**              | `⟨1,0⟩, ⟨0,0⟩, ⟨1,1⟩` (leaf–centre–leaf) | `longest_K_1_3`    |
| `K_{1,1,1}`  | 3   | 1   | **3**              | `⟨0,0⟩, ⟨1,0⟩, ⟨2,0⟩` (triangle)         | `longest_K_1_1_1`  |
| `K_{2,2}`    | 4   | 2   | **4**              | `⟨0,0⟩, ⟨1,0⟩, ⟨0,1⟩, ⟨1,1⟩` (4-cycle)   | `longest_K_2_2`    |

`K_{1,3}` is limited by the `2(N−M)+1` regime, while `K_{1,1,1}` and `K_{2,2}`
are limited by the `N` regime — so both regimes of the `min` are realised and the
bound is sharp.

## 5. An independent enumeration check

To cross-validate the closed form we also implement a fully computable
brute-force enumerator (`bruteMaxLen`): it lists every ordering of every subset
of vertices, keeps the genuine paths, and returns the maximum length.

```lean
def bruteMaxLen : ℕ :=
  (((allVertices n).sublists.flatMap List.permutations).filter (isPathB n)).foldr
    (fun l acc => max l.length acc) 0
```

The Boolean path-checker used inside is proved faithful to the logical predicate:

```lean
theorem isPathB_iff (l) : isPathB n l = true ↔ IsMPPath n l
```

`native_decide` then confirms the enumerator matches the closed form
`formulaBound = min(N, 2(N−M)+1)` on a range of instances:

| Graph       | `bruteMaxLen` | `min(N, 2(N−M)+1)` |
|-------------|---------------|--------------------|
| `K_{1,3}`   | 3             | 3                  |
| `K_{1,1,1}` | 3             | 3                  |
| `K_{2,2}`   | 4             | 4                  |
| `K_{1,4}`   | 3             | 3                  |
| `K_{2,3}`   | 5             | 5                  |
| `K_{3,3}`   | 6             | 6                  |

captured by `brute_K_1_3`, `brute_K_1_1_1`, `brute_K_2_2`, and
`brute_eq_formula_samples`.

## 6. Index of formal results

All in `Catalog/MultipartitePaths/LongestPath.lean`, namespace `MultipartitePaths`.

- `count_le_ceil` — colour–separation lemma.
- `color_count_le` — fibre bound (vertices per part ≤ part size).
- `length_eq_sum_counts` — path length as a sum of colour counts.
- `length_le_N`, `length_le_two`, `length_le_min` — the two bounds and their min.
- `IsLongest`, `longest_K_1_3`, `longest_K_1_1_1`, `longest_K_2_2` — exact values.
- `allVertices`, `chainB`, `isPathB`, `bruteMaxLen`, `formulaBound` — enumeration.
- `chainB_iff`, `isPathB_iff` — faithfulness of the Boolean checker.
- `brute_K_1_3`, `brute_K_1_1_1`, `brute_K_2_2`, `brute_eq_formula_samples` —
  computational confirmation.

concept.title: The Prime Number Crossword: Filling the Gaps in the Primes
concept.concept_description: Prime gaps — the spaces between consecutive primes — are like empty cells in a crossword puzzle. The gaps are 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, ... (OEIS A001223). The pattern seems random, but the crossword has rules: (1) All prime gaps are even (except the first gap of 1 between 2 and 3). (2) A gap g can only appear at position n if n+g is prime and all of n+1, n+2, ..., n+g-1 are composite. (3) The density of gap g near n is approximately 2*C_2/(g*log(n)) where C_2 is the twin prime constant. Conjecture: The prime gap crossword is uniquely solvable — given the pattern of gaps up to N, the next prime is determined with probability 1 - O(1/log(N)). More precisely, the conditional probability that the next prime after p is p + g, given all primes up to p, is approximately 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p)) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2). This is the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for prime gaps. But the crossword has a surprise: certain gap patterns FORCE the next number. For example, if the gaps near n are 6, 4, 2, 6, then the next gap is almost certainly 4 (the only way to fill the crossword). Test: compute the conditional probabilities for prime gaps up to 10^8 and verify they match the Hardy-Littlewood prediction. Find forcing patterns (gaps that uniquely determine the next prime) and prove they occur with positive density. Impact: prime gaps are not random — they are a solvable crossword puzzle with deterministic rules.

concept.title: Tropical Dreams: The Field with One Element Meets Tropical Geometry
concept.concept_description: The field with one element F_1 is a hypothetical object that would explain why the Weil conjectures have the form they do — as if there were a field with q^0 = 1 element. Tropical geometry replaces addition with min and multiplication with addition. What if these two ideas are the SAME? Conjecture: The tropical semiring (R union {infinity}, min, +) IS the field with one element, in the following precise sense: the category of tropical schemes is equivalent to the category of F_1-schemes. More concretely, a tropical variety over F_1 is a set with a min-plus structure, and its base change to Z (formally, tensor with Z) is a toric variety. The key correspondence: F_1-points of a tropical variety are the vertices of its Newton polytope, and the 'cardinality' of the tropical variety (as an F_1-object) is the number of lattice points in the polytope, which equals the degree of the toric variety after base change. Test: for each toric variety corresponding to a polytope P, compute the number of F_1-points (vertices of P) and verify that the Euler characteristic of the toric variety equals |vertices(P)| = #F_1-points. Prove the tensor product correspondence: tropical scheme X over F_1 has X tensor_Z Z = the corresponding toric variety. Impact: F_1 and tropical geometry are two faces of the same coin. The field with one element is tropical, and tropical geometry is the geometry of F_1.

# Future Directions: Tensor Amplification and Spectral Transfer for Sidorenko-Type Inequalities

This cycle established a tensor-amplification engine for Sidorenko-type inequalities on weighted
graphs: closed-walk counts are multiplicative under the tensor product (spectral transfer), the
Sidorenko ratio is therefore multiplicative, the Sidorenko property is closed under tensor products

Principle II). The even cycles `C₂` and `C₄` were shown to satisfy Sidorenko for *all* symmetric
weightings — with no positivity hypothesis — seeding an entire tensor-closed class. The following

the entries of `Aᵐ`, so a chain of `m` Cauchy–Schwarz steps — each passing from `Aʳ` to `A^{2r}`

theorem sq_symm (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (hsym : ∀ i j, A i j = A j i) :
    ∀ i j, (A ^ 2) i j = (A ^ 2) j i := by
  intro i j
  simp only [pow_two, Matrix.mul_apply]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun k _ => ?_)
  rw [hsym i k, hsym k j, mul_comm]

/-- The total weight of `A²` equals the sum of squared column sums of `A`. -/
theorem sum_sq_eq (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (hsym : ∀ i j, A i j = A j i) :
    ∑ i, ∑ j, (A ^ 2) i j = ∑ k, (∑ i, A i k) ^ 2 := by
  simp only [pow_two, Matrix.mul_apply]
  have step : ∀ i : ι, (∑ j, ∑ k, A i k * A k j) = ∑ k, ∑ j, A i k * A k j :=
    fun _ => Finset.sum_comm
  simp only [step]
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun k _ => ?_)
  rw [← Finset.sum_mul_sum]
  congr 1
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun j _ => hsym k j)

/-- **Sidorenko for the 4-cycle `C₄`.** Every symmetric weighted graph satisfies
`t(C₄, A) ≥ t(K₂, A)⁴`. -/
theorem sidorenko_four (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (hsym : ∀ i j, A i j = A j i) :
    Sidorenko 4 A := by
  unfold Sidorenko tEdge tCycle homEdge homCycle

  have hTr : trace (A ^ 4) = ∑ i, ∑ j, ((A ^ 2) i j) ^ 2 := by
    rw [hA4, trace_sq_symm (A ^ 2) (sq_symm A hsym)]

  set T : ℝ := ∑ i, ∑ j, (A ^ 2) i j with hTdef
  have hk1 : T ^ 2 ≤ N ^ 2 * Tr := by rw [hTr]; exact sq_homEdge_le (A ^ 2)
  have hmid : T = ∑ k, (∑ i, A i k) ^ 2 := sum_sq_eq A hsym
  have hSc : S = ∑ k, (∑ i, A i k) := by rw [hS]; exact Finset.sum_comm
  have hk2 : S ^ 2 ≤ N * T := by
    have h := sq_sum_le_card_mul_sum_sq (s := (Finset.univ : Finset ι))
      (f := fun k => ∑ i, A i k)
    rw [Finset.card_univ] at h
    rw [hSc, hmid]; convert h using 2
  have hT0 : 0 ≤ T := by rw [hmid]; exact Finset.sum_nonneg (fun k _ => sq_nonneg _)
  have hNnn : (0 : ℝ) ≤ N := by positivity
  rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hNnn with h0 | hpos
  · rw [← h0]; simp
  · rw [div_pow, div_le_div_iff₀ (by positivity) (by positivity)]
    have e1 : N ^ 6 * T ^ 2 ≤ N ^ 6 * (N ^ 2 * Tr) :=
      mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hk1 (by positivity)

      mul_le_mul hk2 hk2 (sq_nonneg S) (mul_nonneg hNnn hT0)
    have e2 : N ^ 4 * (S ^ 2 * S ^ 2) ≤ N ^ 4 * ((N * T) * (N * T)) :=
      mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hSq4 (by positivity)

/-- The tensor product of two symmetric weighted graphs is symmetric. -/
theorem kron_symm {κ : Type*} (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ)
    (hA : ∀ i j, A i j = A j i) (hB : ∀ i j, B i j = B j i) :
    ∀ p q : ι × κ, (A ⊗ₖ B) p q = (A ⊗ₖ B) q p := by
  intro p q
  simp only [Matrix.kroneckerMap_apply]
  rw [hA, hB]

/-- **Closure of the `C₄`-Sidorenko class.** The tensor product of two symmetric weighted graphs
again satisfies `C₄`-Sidorenko: the analytic seed propagates through the even-cycle tensor transfer
principle, with no positivity assumption anywhere. -/
theorem sidorenko_four_kron {κ : Type*} [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ]
    (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ)
    (hAs : ∀ i j, A i j = A j i) (hBs : ∀ i j, B i j = B j i) :
    Sidorenko 4 (A ⊗ₖ B) :=
  Sidorenko_kron_even (by decide) (sidorenko_four A hAs) (sidorenko_four B hBs)

# Tensor amplification and spectral transfer for Sidorenko-type inequalities

This file develops the **tensor-amplification framework** for Sidorenko-type inequalities in the
setting of *weighted graphs* (finite graphons represented by a square nonnegative matrix over an
arbitrary finite vertex space with the counting measure).  A weighted graph on a finite vertex
space `ι` is a matrix `A : Matrix ι ι ℝ`; its two fundamental homomorphism densities are

* the **edge density** `tEdge A = (∑ i j, A i j) / |ι|²`, the density of the single edge `K₂`, and
* the **cycle density** `tCycle k A = tr(Aᵏ) / |ι|ᵏ`, the density of the `k`-cycle `Cₖ`
  (the number of closed walks of length `k` is `tr(Aᵏ)`).

A weighted graph is said to satisfy the **Sidorenko property for `Cₖ`** when
`tEdge A ^ k ≤ tCycle k A`, i.e. the cycle density is at least the edge density raised to the
number of edges of the cycle.  This is the discrete, uniform-measure incarnation of Sidorenko's
conjecture (see Erdős–Simonovits 1984 and Sidorenko's programme; the graphon language is that of
Lovász–Szegedy 2006, and the amplification philosophy underlies Conlon–Fox–Sudakov 2010 and the
tensor-power arguments revisited by Li–Szegedy 2026).

## Main results

* `homCycle_kron` : **spectral transfer** — closed-walk counts are multiplicative under the tensor
  (Kronecker) product, `tr((A ⊗ B)ᵏ) = tr(Aᵏ)·tr(Bᵏ)`.  This is the algebraic heart of the whole
  framework: tensoring graphons multiplies their cycle spectra.
* `tCycle_kron`, `tEdge_kron` : both densities factor through the tensor product.
* `sidRatio_kron` : the **Sidorenko ratio** `tCycle k A / tEdge A ^ k` is *multiplicative* under the
  tensor product.
* `Sidorenko_kron` : **Transfer Principle I (structural closure)** — the class of weighted graphs
  satisfying the Sidorenko property for `Cₖ` is closed under tensor products.
* `sidRatio_amplify_gt` / `sidRatio_amplify_lt` : **Transfer Principle II (amplification)** — a
  strict surplus (`ratio > 1`) is strictly amplified by self-tensoring, while a strict deficit
  (`0 < ratio < 1`, a Sidorenko violation) is strictly amplified towards `0`.  Thus tensoring is a
  *contraction towards the two fixed points* `0` and `1`, and *any* violation, however small,
  witnesses arbitrarily large violations.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Sidorenko-type inequalities should be governed by a single scalar
  invariant, the Sidorenko ratio `tCycle / tEdge^k`, which is *multiplicative* under a natural
  product on graphons.  If so, the property "ratio ≥ 1" is automatically closed under that product,
  and strict surpluses/deficits must be amplified — turning any counterexample into a family of
  ever-worse counterexamples.
Experiment (Experimenter): Chose the tensor (Kronecker) product as the graphon product.  The
  spectral transfer lemma `tr((A ⊗ B)ᵏ) = tr(Aᵏ)·tr(Bᵏ)` follows from `(A ⊗ B)ᵏ = Aᵏ ⊗ Bᵏ`

import Mathlib

open Matrix BigOperators
open scoped Kronecker

namespace TensorSidorenko

variable {ι κ : Type*} [Fintype ι] [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq ι] [DecidableEq κ]

/-- Homomorphism count of a single edge `K₂`: the sum of all edge weights. -/
def homEdge (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, ∑ j, A i j

/-- Homomorphism count of the `k`-cycle `Cₖ`: the number of closed walks of length `k`,
equal to `tr(Aᵏ)`. -/
def homCycle (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : ℝ := trace (A ^ k)

/-- Edge density: `homEdge` normalised by the number of ordered vertex pairs. -/
noncomputable def tEdge (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : ℝ := homEdge A / (Fintype.card ι : ℝ) ^ 2

/-- Cycle density: `homCycle` normalised by the number of length-`k` vertex tuples. -/
noncomputable def tCycle (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : ℝ :=
  homCycle k A / (Fintype.card ι : ℝ) ^ k

/-- The Sidorenko ratio of a weighted graph for the cycle `Cₖ`. -/
noncomputable def sidRatio (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : ℝ := tCycle k A / (tEdge A) ^ k

/-- The Sidorenko property for the cycle `Cₖ`: the cycle density dominates the `k`-th power of the
edge density. -/
def Sidorenko (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) : Prop := (tEdge A) ^ k ≤ tCycle k A

/-- Powers of a tensor product factor: `(A ⊗ B)ᵏ = Aᵏ ⊗ Bᵏ`. -/
theorem kron_pow (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
    (A ⊗ₖ B) ^ k = (A ^ k) ⊗ₖ (B ^ k) := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ p ih => rw [pow_succ, pow_succ, pow_succ, ih, Matrix.mul_kronecker_mul]

/-- **Spectral transfer.** Closed-walk counts are multiplicative under the tensor product:
`tr((A ⊗ B)ᵏ) = tr(Aᵏ)·tr(Bᵏ)`.  Tensoring graphons multiplies their cycle spectra. -/
theorem homCycle_kron (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) :
    homCycle k (A ⊗ₖ B) = homCycle k A * homCycle k B := by
  unfold homCycle
  rw [kron_pow, trace_kronecker]

omit [DecidableEq ι] [DecidableEq κ] in
/-- The edge count is multiplicative under the tensor product. -/
theorem homEdge_kron (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) :
    homEdge (A ⊗ₖ B) = homEdge A * homEdge B := by
  unfold homEdge
  simp only [Matrix.kroneckerMap_apply, Fintype.sum_prod_type]
  rw [Finset.sum_mul_sum]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i _ => Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i' _ => ?_))
  rw [Finset.sum_mul_sum]

/-- Cycle density factors through the tensor product. -/
theorem tCycle_kron (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) :
    tCycle k (A ⊗ₖ B) = tCycle k A * tCycle k B := by
  unfold tCycle
  rw [homCycle_kron, Fintype.card_prod]
  push_cast
  rw [mul_pow, div_mul_div_comm]

omit [DecidableEq ι] [DecidableEq κ] in
/-- Edge density factors through the tensor product. -/
theorem tEdge_kron (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) :
    tEdge (A ⊗ₖ B) = tEdge A * tEdge B := by
  unfold tEdge
  rw [homEdge_kron, Fintype.card_prod]
  push_cast
  rw [mul_pow, div_mul_div_comm]

/-- The Sidorenko ratio is multiplicative under the tensor product. -/
theorem sidRatio_kron (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (B : Matrix κ κ ℝ) :
    sidRatio k (A ⊗ₖ B) = sidRatio k A * sidRatio k B := by
  unfold sidRatio
  rw [tCycle_kron, tEdge_kron, mul_pow, div_mul_div_comm]

omit [DecidableEq ι] in
/-- A nonnegative weighted graph has nonnegative edge count. -/
theorem homEdge_nonneg {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} (hA : ∀ i j, 0 ≤ A i j) : 0 ≤ homEdge A := by
  unfold homEdge
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg (fun i _ => Finset.sum_nonneg (fun j _ => hA i j))

omit [DecidableEq ι] in
/-- A nonnegative weighted graph has nonnegative edge density. -/
theorem tEdge_nonneg {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} (hA : ∀ i j, 0 ≤ A i j) : 0 ≤ tEdge A := by
  unfold tEdge
  exact div_nonneg (homEdge_nonneg hA) (by positivity)

/-- **Transfer Principle I (structural closure).** The class of weighted graphs satisfying the
Sidorenko property for `Cₖ` is closed under tensor products. -/
theorem Sidorenko_kron {k : ℕ} {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} {B : Matrix κ κ ℝ}
    (hA : Sidorenko k A) (hB : Sidorenko k B)
    (hA0 : 0 ≤ tEdge A) (hB0 : 0 ≤ tEdge B) :
    Sidorenko k (A ⊗ₖ B) := by
  unfold Sidorenko at *
  rw [tCycle_kron, tEdge_kron, mul_pow]
  exact mul_le_mul hA hB (pow_nonneg hB0 k) (le_trans (pow_nonneg hA0 k) hA)

/-- **Transfer Principle I for even cycles.** For an *even* cycle length the Sidorenko property is
closed under tensor products with no positivity hypothesis whatsoever: an even power of the edge
density is automatically nonnegative, so the two Sidorenko inequalities multiply directly. -/
theorem Sidorenko_kron_even {k : ℕ} (hk : Even k) {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} {B : Matrix κ κ ℝ}
    (hA : Sidorenko k A) (hB : Sidorenko k B) :
    Sidorenko k (A ⊗ₖ B) := by
  unfold Sidorenko at *
  rw [tCycle_kron, tEdge_kron, mul_pow]
  exact mul_le_mul hA hB (hk.pow_nonneg _) (le_trans (hk.pow_nonneg _) hA)

/-- Self-tensoring squares the Sidorenko ratio. -/
theorem sidRatio_self_kron (k : ℕ) (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) :
    sidRatio k (A ⊗ₖ A) = (sidRatio k A) ^ 2 := by
  rw [sidRatio_kron, sq]

/-- **Transfer Principle II (amplification of surplus).** A strict Sidorenko surplus is strictly
amplified by self-tensoring. -/
theorem sidRatio_amplify_gt {k : ℕ} {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} (h : 1 < sidRatio k A) :
    sidRatio k A < sidRatio k (A ⊗ₖ A) := by
  rw [sidRatio_self_kron, sq]
  nlinarith [h]

/-- **Transfer Principle II (amplification of deficit).** A strict Sidorenko *violation*
(`0 < ratio < 1`) is strictly amplified towards `0` by self-tensoring: violations compound. -/
theorem sidRatio_amplify_lt {k : ℕ} {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ}
    (h0 : 0 < sidRatio k A) (h1 : sidRatio k A < 1) :
    sidRatio k (A ⊗ₖ A) < sidRatio k A := by
  rw [sidRatio_self_kron, sq]
  nlinarith [h0, h1]

/-- The two fixed points of amplification: `ratio = 1` is preserved by self-tensoring
(the sharp/extremal case). -/
theorem sidRatio_fixed_one {k : ℕ} {A : Matrix ι ι ℝ} (h : sidRatio k A = 1) :
    sidRatio k (A ⊗ₖ A) = 1 := by
  rw [sidRatio_self_kron, h, one_pow]

end TensorSidorenko

1fb61210-87eb-4018-bc6d-2a8930947c61.result_demo:
"""
Numerical demonstrations for
"Tensor Amplification and Spectral Transfer for Sidorenko-Type Inequalities".

A *weighted graph* is a symmetric real matrix A (the vertex space carries the
uniform/counting measure).  We work with two homomorphism densities:

    edge density   t(K2, A) = (1/N^2) * sum_{i,j} A[i,j]
    cycle density  t(Ck, A) = (1/N^k) * trace(A^k)

The Sidorenko property for the k-cycle is  t(Ck, A) >= t(K2, A)^k, equivalently
the Sidorenko ratio  R_k(A) = t(Ck, A) / t(K2, A)^k  satisfies R_k(A) >= 1.

This script demonstrates, with no external dependencies:
  * the sign-free even-cycle base cases (C2 and C4),
  * spectral transfer: densities and the ratio are multiplicative under the
    Kronecker (tensor) product,
  * amplification: self-tensoring squares the ratio (orbit R, R^2, R^4, ...).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List


Matrix = List[List[float]]


def n_vertices(A: Matrix) -> int:
    """Number of vertices (rows) of a square weighted graph."""
    return len(A)


def is_symmetric(A: Matrix, tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    """Check A[i][j] == A[j][i] within tolerance."""
    n = n_vertices(A)
    return all(abs(A[i][j] - A[j][i]) <= tol for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


def mat_mul(A: Matrix, B: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Naive matrix product of two square matrices of equal size."""
    n = n_vertices(A)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(n)]
            for i in range(n)]


def mat_pow(A: Matrix, k: int) -> Matrix:
    """k-th matrix power by repeated squaring (k >= 0)."""
    n = n_vertices(A)
    result: Matrix = [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    base = [row[:] for row in A]
    while k > 0:
        if k & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        k >>= 1
    return result


def trace(A: Matrix) -> float:
    """Sum of the diagonal entries."""
    return sum(A[i][i] for i in range(n_vertices(A)))


def total_weight(A: Matrix) -> float:
    """Sum of all entries = hom(K2, A)."""
    return sum(sum(row) for row in A)


def t_edge(A: Matrix) -> float:
    """Edge density t(K2, A)."""
    n = n_vertices(A)
    return total_weight(A) / (n ** 2)


def t_cycle(k: int, A: Matrix) -> float:
    """Cycle density t(Ck, A) = trace(A^k) / N^k."""
    n = n_vertices(A)
    return trace(mat_pow(A, k)) / (n ** k)


def sid_ratio(k: int, A: Matrix) -> float:
    """Sidorenko ratio R_k(A) = t(Ck, A) / t(K2, A)^k."""
    return t_cycle(k, A) / (t_edge(A) ** k)


def kron(A: Matrix, B: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Kronecker (tensor) product: vertices are pairs, weights multiply."""
    na, nb = n_vertices(A), n_vertices(B)
    n = na * nb
    C: Matrix = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(na):
        for j in range(na):
            for ip in range(nb):
                for jp in range(nb):
                    C[i * nb + ip][j * nb + jp] = A[i][j] * B[ip][jp]
    return C


def demo_base_cases() -> None:
    """C2 and C4 Sidorenko hold for symmetric graphs, including signed ones."""
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Base cases: sign-free even-cycle Sidorenko (C2 and C4)")
    print("=" * 68)
    examples = {
        "random-like positive": [[0.3, 0.7, 0.2],
                                 [0.7, 0.5, 0.9],
                                 [0.2, 0.9, 0.4]],
        "SIGNED (has negatives)": [[1.0, -2.0, 0.5],
                                   [-2.0, 3.0, -1.0],
                                   [0.5, -1.0, 2.0]],
        "constant (extremal)": [[0.6, 0.6], [0.6, 0.6]],
    }
    for name, A in examples.items():
        assert is_symmetric(A)
        r2, r4 = sid_ratio(2, A), sid_ratio(4, A)
        print(f"\n{name}:")
        print(f"  t(K2)={t_edge(A):+.4f}  t(C2)={t_cycle(2, A):+.4f}  "
              f"t(C4)={t_cycle(4, A):+.4f}")
        print(f"  R2 = {r2:.6f}  (>= 1 ? {r2 >= 1 - 1e-9})")
        print(f"  R4 = {r4:.6f}  (>= 1 ? {r4 >= 1 - 1e-9})")


def demo_spectral_transfer() -> None:
    """Densities and the ratio are multiplicative under the tensor product."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 68)
    print("Spectral transfer: multiplicativity under tensor product")
    print("=" * 68)
    A = [[0.4, 0.5], [0.5, 0.8]]
    B = [[0.2, 0.9, 0.1], [0.9, 0.3, 0.6], [0.1, 0.6, 0.7]]
    AB = kron(A, B)
    for k in (2, 4):
        lhs = t_cycle(k, AB)
        rhs = t_cycle(k, A) * t_cycle(k, B)
        print(f"\nk = {k}:")
        print(f"  t(C{k}, A(x)B)         = {lhs:.8f}")
        print(f"  t(C{k}, A) * t(C{k}, B) = {rhs:.8f}   match: {abs(lhs-rhs) < 1e-9}")
        rl, rr = sid_ratio(k, AB), sid_ratio(k, A) * sid_ratio(k, B)

# Computational Evidence: Tensor Amplification and Spectral Transfer

All computations use the weighted-graph model: a weighted graph on `n` vertices is a symmetric
`n × n` matrix `A`, with edge density `t(K₂,A) = (∑ᵢⱼ Aᵢⱼ)/n²` and cycle density
`t(Cₖ,A) = tr(Aᵏ)/nᵏ`.

## 1. Small-case calculations

Take the symmetric weighted graph
```
A = [ 1  2 ]
    [ 2  3 ]      (n = 2)
```
Then `∑ᵢⱼ Aᵢⱼ = 8`, `tr(A²) = 18`, `tr(A⁴) = 322`, so

| quantity            | value |
|---------------------|-------|
| edge density `t(K₂)`| `8/4 = 2` |
| `C₂` density `t(C₂)`| `18/4 = 9/2` |
| `C₄` density `t(C₄)`| `322/16 = 161/8` |

* **C₂ surplus** `t(C₂) − t(K₂)² = 9/2 − 4 = 1/2 > 0`  ✔
* **C₄ surplus** `t(C₄) − t(K₂)⁴ = 161/8 − 16 = 33/8 > 0`  ✔

Both even-cycle Sidorenko inequalities hold strictly on this example, consistent with
`sidorenko_two` and `sidorenko_four`.

## 2. Spectral transfer (tensor multiplicativity)

For the same `A`, direct computation gives
```
tr((A ⊗ A)³) − tr(A³)²  =  0
tr((A ⊗ A)⁴) − tr(A⁴)²  =  0
```
confirming the identity `tr((A ⊗ B)ᵏ) = tr(Aᵏ)·tr(Bᵏ)` (theorem `homCycle_kron`) — the algebraic
heart of the framework.

## 3. Amplification

Because the Sidorenko ratio `R = t(Cₖ)/t(K₂)ᵏ` is multiplicative under the tensor product, the
self-tensor square satisfies `R(A ⊗ A) = R(A)²`. For the example above with `k = 4`,
`R(A) = (161/8)/16 = 161/128 ≈ 1.258 > 1`, and `R(A ⊗ A) = R(A)² ≈ 1.582 > R(A)`: a genuine
surplus is strictly amplified, matching `sidRatio_amplify_gt`. A deficit `0 < R < 1` would instead
be driven towards `0` (`sidRatio_amplify_lt`).

## 4. Counterexample hunt

The even-cycle claims were tested on random symmetric integer matrices of sizes `n = 2,3,4`
(including matrices with negative entries): the `C₂` and `C₄` surpluses were nonnegative in every
case, in agreement with the sign-free proofs. Odd cycles were deliberately excluded — `C₃` violates
Sidorenko for suitable weightings, matching the classical bipartite restriction — so no odd-cycle
claim is made.

## Summary

The computational evidence supports (a) both even-cycle base inequalities, (b) exact tensor
multiplicativity of closed-walk counts, and (c) the multiplicative amplification law for the
Sidorenko ratio. All three are established rigorously in the accompanying development.

# Future Directions: Tensor Amplification and Spectral Transfer for Sidorenko-Type Inequalities

This cycle established a tensor-amplification engine for Sidorenko-type inequalities on weighted
graphs: closed-walk counts are multiplicative under the tensor product (spectral transfer), the
Sidorenko ratio is therefore multiplicative, the Sidorenko property is closed under tensor products
(Transfer Principle I), and surpluses/deficits are strictly amplified by self-tensoring (Transfer
Principle II). The even cycles `C₂` and `C₄` were shown to satisfy Sidorenko for *all* symmetric
weightings — with no positivity hypothesis — seeding an entire tensor-closed class. The following
conjectures grow directly out of these findings.

## Conjecture 1 (Sign-free even-cycle Sidorenko for all lengths)

Every even cycle `C₂ₘ` satisfies `t(C₂ₘ, A) ≥ t(K₂, A)^{2m}` for every symmetric weighted graph
`A`, with no assumption on the signs of the entries.

*The key insight is* that the closed-walk count `tr(A^{2m})` is intrinsically a sum of squares of
the entries of `Aᵐ`, so a chain of `m` Cauchy–Schwarz steps — each passing from `Aʳ` to `A^{2r}`
through the squared row sums — never inspects a sign; the nonnegativity usually imposed on graphons
is a red herring for even cycles.

*Why now?* The `C₄` case was just proved in exactly this sign-free, doubling form, exposing the
recursive `Aʳ ↦ A^{2r}` structure. Turning that one step into an induction on `m` is the natural
and immediate next target, and it would settle the even-cycle case of Sidorenko in the discrete
model in one stroke.

## Conjecture 2 (Amplification dichotomy and the ratio spectrum)

Under the tensor product the Sidorenko ratio behaves as a discrete dynamical system with exactly
two fixed points, `0` and `1`: for a fixed cycle `Cₖ`, the closure of the set of achievable ratios
`{R(A)}` under multiplication is the whole interval `[0, ∞)`, and iterated self-tensoring sends
every `R ≠ 1` monotonically to a fixed point (`R > 1 → ∞`, `0 < R < 1 → 0`).

*The key insight is* that multiplicativity of the ratio converts a single graph with `R ≠ 1` into a
geometric orbit `R, R², R⁴, …`, so the *existence* of any surplus or deficit, however tiny, already
witnesses arbitrarily extreme behaviour — the inequality has no "almost-tight" regime that is
stable under tensoring.

*Why now?* The multiplicativity identity and both strict amplification laws are now in hand; what
remains is to characterise which ratios are realizable and to prove the orbit-closure statement,
making the qualitative "amplification" picture into a precise structural theorem.

## Conjecture 3 (Spectral transfer beyond cycles)

The multiplicativity `t(H, A ⊗ B) = t(H, A)·t(H, B)` holds for *every* pattern graph `H`, not only
cycles, and consequently the Sidorenko property for any bipartite `H` is closed under tensor
products and its ratio is amplified by self-tensoring.

*The key insight is* that homomorphism counts are contractions of tensor powers of the adjacency
operator, and the Kronecker product acts diagonally on every such contraction, so multiplicativity
is a property of the pattern-independent tensor structure rather than of the special trace formula
for cycles.

*Why now?* The cycle case reduced entirely to `(A ⊗ B)ᵏ = Aᵏ ⊗ Bᵏ` together with multiplicativity
of the trace; the same two ingredients, applied to the general homomorphism-count functional,
should yield the pattern-independent statement and thereby a uniform tensor-closure principle for
all of Sidorenko's conjecture.

## Conjecture 4 (Extremal rigidity of the tight case)

For an even cycle `Cₖ`, equality `t(Cₖ, A) = t(K₂, A)ᵏ` forces `A` to be a constant weighting (a
rescaled complete looped graph), and this rigidity is preserved and detected by the tensor product:
`R(A) = 1` if and only if `A` is constant.

*The key insight is* that each Cauchy–Schwarz step in the even-cycle proof is tight exactly when
the relevant vectors are proportional to the all-ones vector, so equality throughout propagates
back to constancy of the original weighting, and the fixed point `R = 1` of the amplification map
corresponds precisely to the extremal graphons.

*Why now?* The proof of `C₄` already isolates the exact Cauchy–Schwarz steps whose equality cases
must be analysed, and the amplification map's fixed point at `1` gives an independent, dynamical
handle on the extremal set; combining the two should convert the inequalities into rigidity
theorems.

# When Small Advantages Snowball: The Tensor Trick Behind Sidorenko's Conjecture

## A question about counting patterns

Imagine you are handed a large network — a social graph, a molecule, a grid of
correlations — and asked a deceptively simple question: *how many times does a
particular small pattern appear inside it?* A single edge. A triangle. A square
loop of four vertices. Counting patterns inside larger structures is one of the
oldest games in combinatorics, and it turns out to secretly govern everything
from statistical physics to the design of error-correcting codes.

One of the most famous open problems in this game is **Sidorenko's conjecture**.
In plain language it says something that sounds almost obvious but is fiendishly
hard to prove in general: *among all networks with a fixed edge density, the
random-looking ones contain the fewest copies of any bipartite pattern.*
Randomness minimizes structure. If you know only how dense a network is, you can
guarantee at least as many copies of a loop, a path, or a tree as a purely
random network of the same density would have — never fewer.

This article is about a clean and surprisingly powerful idea for attacking
inequalities of this kind: a **tensor-amplification framework**. The slogan is
that tiny advantages *compound*, and that a single algebraic identity — how
loops multiply when you take a certain product of networks — turns two hard-looking
principles into near-trivialities.

## Networks as matrices

To make the counting precise, we represent a network on a set of vertices by a
square table of numbers, a **weighted graph** $A$, where the entry $A_{ij}$ is
the weight of the connection between vertices $i$ and $j$. We only ask that the
table be *symmetric*: $A_{ij} = A_{ji}$, meaning the connection from $i$ to $j$
is the same as from $j$ to $i$. Nothing more. In particular we do **not** require
the weights to be positive — a subtlety that will pay off handsomely later.

Two "densities" summarize how patterns sit inside $A$. Write $N$ for the number
of vertices. The **edge density**
$$t(K_2, A) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i}\sum_{j} A_{ij}$$
is just the average connection strength. The **cycle density**
$$t(C_k, A) = \frac{1}{N^k}\,\mathrm{tr}(A^k)$$
counts closed walks of length $k$ — chains of steps that leave a vertex and
return after exactly $k$ moves — normalized by the number of possible walks.
Here $\mathrm{tr}(A^k)$, the trace of the $k$-th matrix power, is exactly the
total number of such closed walks, a classical fact from linear algebra.

For an even loop $C_k$, the **Sidorenko property** is the clean inequality
$$t(C_k, A) \;\ge\; t(K_2, A)^k.$$
The number of loops is at least the edge density raised to the number of edges
in the loop. This is Sidorenko's conjecture, made concrete for cycles.

## The multiplication that changes everything

Here is the pivot. Given two weighted graphs $A$ and $B$, form their **tensor
product** $A \otimes B$. Its vertices are *pairs* — one vertex from each factor —
and the weight of the connection between the pair $(i, i')$ and the pair $(j, j')$
is simply the product $A_{ij}\,B_{i'j'}$. This is the natural way to overlay two
networks into one much larger composite network.

The magic is what tensoring does to loop counts. A closed walk in the composite
is precisely a closed walk in the first factor *paired with* a closed walk in the
second. Counting them therefore **multiplies**:
$$\mathrm{tr}\big((A\otimes B)^k\big) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(A^k)\cdot\mathrm{tr}(B^k).$$
We call this the **Spectral Transfer** identity, because it says the entire
"cycle spectrum" of the product is the product of the spectra. The same
multiplicativity holds for the edge counts, and once you fold in the fact that
the product has $N_A \cdot N_B$ vertices, *every* normalized density factors:
$$t(C_k, A\otimes B) = t(C_k, A)\,t(C_k, B), \qquad
t(K_2, A\otimes B) = t(K_2, A)\,t(K_2, B).$$

## The Sidorenko ratio and its two magnets

Now define a single number that captures how well a network obeys Sidorenko's
inequality — its **Sidorenko ratio**:
$$R(A) = \frac{t(C_k, A)}{t(K_2, A)^k}.$$
The Sidorenko property is exactly the statement $R(A) \ge 1$. A network with
$R(A) = 1$ sits precisely on the boundary; $R(A) > 1$ has a *surplus* of loops;
and $R(A) < 1$ would be a genuine *violation* of the conjecture.

Because every density is multiplicative under tensoring, the ratio is too:
$$R(A\otimes B) = R(A)\cdot R(B).$$
This one line is the engine of the whole theory, and it immediately delivers two
principles.

**Transfer Principle I — closure.** If two networks both satisfy Sidorenko, so
does their product. Indeed, if $R(A) \ge 1$ and $R(B) \ge 1$ then
$R(A\otimes B) = R(A)R(B) \ge 1$. The class of Sidorenko-obeying networks is
*closed* under tensoring; you can never leave it by multiplying.

**Transfer Principle II — amplification.** Self-tensor a network with itself and
its ratio *squares*:
$$R(A\otimes A) = R(A)^2.$$
Iterate, and you get the geometric orbit $R, R^2, R^4, R^8, \dots$. Now watch the
dynamics. The map $x \mapsto x^2$ has exactly two fixed points, $0$ and $1$. A
surplus $R > 1$ is flung off to infinity; a deficit $0 < R < 1$ is dragged
inexorably to zero. The value $R = 1$ — the sharp, extremal, random-like case —
sits perfectly balanced between them.

The moral is striking: **there is no such thing as a small violation.** If any
network anywhere had a Sidorenko ratio even a hair below $1$, tensoring it with
itself repeatedly would manufacture violations as extreme as you like. Any crack
in the conjecture, however faint, would widen into a chasm.

## Seeding the machine: loops of length two and four

A machine that transforms Sidorenko-obeying networks into new ones is useless
unless you can feed it something to start with. So the framework is seeded with
two rock-solid base cases, both proved by nothing more exotic than the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality — the workhorse that says a sum of products is never
larger than what you get by separating the two factors.

**The two-cycle.** Every symmetric weighted graph satisfies
$$t(C_2, A) \ge t(K_2, A)^2.$$
Why? The trace $\mathrm{tr}(A^2)$ equals the sum of *squared* weights,
$\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz applied to the $N^2$ ordered pairs says the
square of the total weight is at most $N^2$ times the sum of squared weights:
$$\Big(\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}\Big)^2 \le N^2 \sum_{i,j} A_{ij}^2.$$
Divide through by the right normalizing powers of $N$ and the inequality is
exactly $C_2$-Sidorenko.

**The four-cycle.** Every symmetric weighted graph satisfies
$$t(C_4, A) \ge t(K_2, A)^4.$$
The proof chains two Cauchy–Schwarz steps through an intermediate quantity. The
trace $\mathrm{tr}(A^4) = \mathrm{tr}((A^2)^2)$ is again a sum of squares, this
time of the entries of $A^2$. One Cauchy–Schwarz bounds it below in terms of the
total weight of $A^2$; a second bounds that total weight — which equals the sum
of squared column sums of $A$ — below in terms of the total weight of $A$. Stitch
the two together and $C_4$-Sidorenko falls out.

Here is the beautiful part, and the reason we insisted only on symmetry. **Neither
proof ever looks at the sign of a single weight.** Every intermediate quantity —
sums of squares, squared column sums, traces of even powers — is automatically
nonnegative. The positivity condition that is usually imposed on these problems
turns out, for even loops, to be a red herring. The inequalities hold for *all*
symmetric real weightings, negative entries and all. And they are sharp: constant
networks achieve equality, so nothing has been given away.

## Putting it together

Combine the seeds with Transfer Principle I and something lovely emerges. Start
with the four-cycle base case. Tensor copies of your networks together in any
combination. Every product you build still satisfies the four-cycle Sidorenko
inequality — automatically, and again with no positivity assumption. From two
analytic seeds and one algebraic identity you generate an *entire tensor-closed
universe* of networks obeying Sidorenko's conjecture for the four-cycle.

Why stop at four? The four-cycle proof already reveals a recursive skeleton:
pass from $A^r$ to $A^{2r}$ by a single Cauchy–Schwarz step that never inspects a
sign. Turning that one step into an induction is the natural route to proving the
sign-free Sidorenko inequality for *every* even loop $C_{2m}$ — a tantalizing and
concrete next target.

## Why it matters

Inequalities like Sidorenko's are not abstract curiosities. Homomorphism-density
inequalities underpin the theory of quasirandomness (why do pseudorandom objects
behave like truly random ones?), extremal graph theory (how much structure can a
network avoid?), and the analysis of large networks through the lens of graph
limits. The tensor-amplification viewpoint reframes a family of hard analytic
inequalities as a single question about a *dynamical system on a ratio*, with two
magnetic fixed points at $0$ and $1$.

The deeper lesson is one that reaches beyond mathematics: in the right
multiplicative world, advantages and disadvantages do not stay small. They
compound. A structure that beats randomness by an eyelash, tensored with itself
enough times, beats it by a landslide — and a structure that falls short, however
slightly, is doomed to fall short catastrophically. Sidorenko's boundary,
$R = 1$, is the knife's edge between these two fates, and understanding why the
random world sits exactly there is what makes the conjecture so enduring.
